senses.gloss:
ūrdhvapuṇḍra
(‘upright or vertical religious mark’)
------------------------------------------
Literally the word means a religious mark (puṇḍra) which is worn upright (ūrdhva). In common parlance, it is called nāma. Since it has been ordained by the Vaiṣṇava scriptures that while marking the various parts of the body with the ऊर्ध्वपुण्ड्र, names of Lord विष्णु (like Keśava) are to be repeated and that the respective mark represents the respective aspect of the Deity indicated by that particular name, the word nāma (= name) has become synonymous with the ऊर्ध्वपुण्ड्र itself. Invariably associated with the शङ्ख or the conch on its left side and the चक्र or the discus on its right side, this forms the chief symbol of the followers of Śrī Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) who are known as Śrīvaiṣṇavas.
Lord विष्णु, the middle deity of the Hindu Trinity, does not seem to have had a very prominent place in the वेदस्. But, by the time the भागवत cult developed (through its basic writings like the Nārāyaṇīya section of the Mahābhārata, the Viṣṇupurāṇa and the Pāncarātra Āgamas as also the famous Bhāgavatam) विष्णु or नारायण had become the most important deity of the Hindu pantheon.
The word विष्णु literally means one who pervades everything, one who has entered into everything. So, विष्णु is the Cosmic Spirit, the Absolute, which pervades everything. For purposes of religious worship and meditation, he is described as endowed with a beautiful form, deep blue in colour. He has four arms wearing शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), गदा (mace) and पद्म (lotus). He wears a jewel, कौस्तुभ, on His chest. Single-minded devotion is the easiest and best means to please Him.
The followers of Viṣṇuism can be broadly divided into two groups: the Sadvaiṣṇavas (or Vaiṣṇavas who are followers of Śrī मध्वाचार्य) and the Śrīvaiṣṇavas. Both of them accept Lord विष्णु as the Supreme Deity and devotion to Him as the chief means of attaining spiritual beatitude. शङ्ख and चक्र as the religious symbols are acceptable to both of them. However, the Śrīvaiṣṇavas add the ऊर्ध्वपुण्ड्र also.
The शङ्ख or the conch has the form of a multiple spiral evolving from one point into ever-increasing spheres. It thus symbolised the origin of the universe from a single source, viz., God. Being found in water, it symbolises the causal waters from which the universe was evolved and into which it gets dissolved. When blown, it produces a sound, which represents the primeval sound from which च्रेअतिओन् developed. It is also taken to be the representation of the Cosmic Ego. Its involute curve can represent, on the plane of the microcosm or the individual, the egoism which involves him in सṁसार or transmigratory existence.
The चक्र or the discus represents the Universal मिन्द्, the unlimited power that creates and destroys all the spheres and forms of the universe, the nature of which is to revolve or to change. It also represents the Lord’s will to multiply. Its six spokes represent the six seasons of the year, hence the changing universe, set on the unchanging axle, the pivot, represented by the magic syllable hrīm of the Lord. The circle round the wheel is māyā, the divine power of इल्लुसिओन्. On the microcosmic plane, it can be taken to be a true representation of the individual’s मिन्द्, which is ever changing like the rotating wheel.
The Hindu religious tradition has always insisted upon its followers to wear religious marks appropriate to their faith, on their bodies, especially on the forehead. ऊर्ध्वपुण्ड्र is one such mark. The meaning and significance of this symbol is rather obscure to discover. When marked on the forehead of the Deity in a temple, it may signify the power of that Deity to uplift the votaries. When marked on the forehead of the votary it may remind him of the need to take a spiritually upward path. It is sometimes interpreted that the two lines on the outside represent the iḍā and the पिङ्गला (the two passages for the flow of prāṇic energy, intertwining the backbone) and the middle line (marked in red or yellow colour) represents the सुषुम्ना passage (through which the कुण्डलिनी power flows after awakening). The three together represent the yogic path of spiritual ascent.
So, the total symbol (the Ūrdhva-पुण्ड्र along with the शङ्ख and the चक्र) may mean that one who aspires after controlling the मिन्द् and subjugating the egoism should take to the propitiation of the Deity’s merciful power or to the Yogic path.
The ऊर्ध्वपुण्ड्र is marked as by the वडगलैस् (the ‘Northerners’) and as by the Teṅgalais (the ‘Southerners’).
Clay, white or yellow, is used for marking the outer lines and turmeric or śrīcūrṇa (a kind of red powder) for marking the central line.
